title: Your weekend was won… not given.
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Karian reads the new Gethin and Saez study 'Global Working Hours', which harmonises about 2,200 labour force surveys across 160 countries, as evidence against the idea that companies can hand people their time back. The headline finding is that prime-age hours have barely moved in 125 years: the average American adult worked about 30 hours a week in 1900 and does so today, although an hour of work now produces more than ten times as much. Hours rise as countries industrialise and fall again only once they are rich enough to regulate, so what shortens working time is law, not wealth or productivity. He lists compulsory schooling, pensions, the statutory week and paid leave as the real reductions, each fought by employers. Drawing on two decades measuring employee experience, he tells leaders to be honest that wellbeing perks make jobs more bearable without returning anyone's life. He closes by noting that the promise that AI will free us from work repeats the claim made for every earlier technology.
points: Hours worked per adult have stayed flat for 125 years even as output per hour rose more than tenfold, so productivity gains have been taken as output and not as leisure.
Working time rises through industrialisation and falls later mainly because wealthy countries legislate on schooling, pensions and working hours, not because wealth itself buys leisure.
Every genuine reduction in working time over the past century came from a law that employers generally resisted, not from voluntary corporate generosity.
Leaders should be honest that flexible-working and wellbeing programmes make work more bearable but do not give anyone their life back.
The promise that AI will free people from work echoes the one made for the steam engine, the spreadsheet and email, which raised output while hours stayed put.
quotes: Hours worked by prime-age adults (everyone aged 20 to 59) have barely moved across the entire course of development. In the United States, prime-age hours were about 30 a week in 1900. They are about 30 a week today.
The point is narrower than that: a trade was made, over and over, and almost nobody decided to make it. There was never a moment where the choice was put to anyone.
So, countries don’t work less as they get richer. They work longer as they industrialise, and shorter once they’re wealthy enough to regulate.
Instead, the definition of a normal life kept rising to meet whatever the economy could produce.
So the twentieth century did not reduce work. It reallocated it. Men handed back hours while women took on paid work wholesale; the household total held roughly steady.
Every genuine reduction in human working time over the past century came from a law. Compulsory education, state pensions, the statutory working week, overtime rules, mandatory paid leave.

If your flexible working policy makes the job more bearable, say that. It’s a real and decent thing. Just don’t claim it’s giving anyone their life back, because the data says the only things that have ever done that arrived via statute, and were opposed by most employers at the time.
Technology has never once decided how much we work. We decide (or rather our respective governments do).
